title: How to Brew Good Coffee
subtitle: A step-by-step guide — and a useful model for giving instructions in English.
description: An A2 reading and listening text explaining how to brew coffee step by step, with practice in imperatives, sequencing words and kitchen vocabulary.
passage: Brewing coffee means getting the flavor and the smell out of ground coffee beans by adding hot water. It sounds simple, and it is — but a few small choices make the difference between a good cup and a disappointing one. Here are the steps.

First, grind the beans. Use fresh beans if you can, and grind them just before you brew. How fine you grind them depends on your method: a French press needs a coarse grind, while an espresso machine needs a very fine one.
Next, heat the water. The best temperature is between 195 and 205 degrees Fahrenheit, which is just below boiling. If the water is boiling hot, it burns the coffee and the taste turns bitter.
Then prepare the filter. If you are using a paper filter, put it in the basket and pour a little hot water through it. This washes out the taste of the paper and warms up the pot at the same time.
Now add the coffee. A good rule of thumb is one to two tablespoons of ground coffee for every six ounces of water. Use more if you like it strong, less if you like it mild.

Pour the water slowly over the grounds, moving in a circle so that all the coffee gets wet. Stop after a few seconds and wait about half a minute. The coffee will rise and bubble a little — this is called the bloom — and then you can add the rest of the water.
How long you wait depends on the method. A French press takes four to five minutes. Drip coffee takes two to four. An espresso machine needs only twenty to thirty seconds.
Finally, take out the filter, throw away the grounds, and pour the coffee into a mug. Drink it while it is hot.
The taste of your coffee depends on the beans, the grind, the water temperature and the time. Change one thing at a time, and you will soon find the cup you like best.

vocabulary.definition: to break something into very small pieces or powder
in large pieces / in very small pieces
to make coffee or tea with hot water
a sharp, unpleasant taste, like very strong coffee
the wet coffee that is left after brewing
a simple, approximate rule that usually works
a large spoon used for measuring in cooking

exercises.title: Understanding the Text
exercises.instructions: The questions use different words from the text. Think about the meaning, not the exact wording.

items.prompt: You are making coffee in a French press. How should the coffee be ground?
items.explanation: A French press needs a coarse grind, and coarse means in large pieces.

items.prompt: Your coffee tastes sharp and unpleasant. According to the text, what is the likely cause?
items.explanation: Boiling water “burns the coffee and the taste turns bitter” — bitter being that sharp, unpleasant taste.

items.prompt: Pouring hot water through the paper filter first does two things. What are they?
options: It cleans the filter and warms the pot
It measures the water and cools the pot
It makes the coffee stronger and darker
items.explanation: It washes out the paper taste and warms the brewing vessel at the same time.

items.prompt: You want a mild cup. What should you do?
items.explanation: “Use more if you like it strong, less if you like it mild.”

items.prompt: Just after the first water goes on, the coffee rises and bubbles. What is that called, and what should you do?
options: The bloom — wait about half a minute
The brew — pour the rest at once
items.explanation: That rising and bubbling is the bloom, and you wait roughly thirty seconds before adding the rest.

items.prompt: Which method finishes in well under a minute?
items.explanation: Espresso takes 20–30 seconds; drip takes 2–4 minutes and a French press 4–5.

items.prompt: Your coffee is not good. What does the text suggest you do?
options: Change one thing and taste again
items.explanation: “Change one thing at a time” — so that you can tell which change made the difference.

exercises.title: True or False?
exercises.instructions: Decide whether each sentence is true. The words are not the same as in the text.

items.statement: It is better to grind the beans well in advance.
items.explanation: False — grind them just before you brew.

items.statement: The water should not quite reach boiling point.
items.explanation: True — 195–205°F is described as just below boiling.

items.statement: All the water goes on in one go.
items.explanation: False — pour some, wait for the bloom, then add the rest.

items.statement: A French press takes longer than drip coffee.
The amount of coffee you use changes how strong it tastes.
items.explanation: True — more for strong, less for mild.

items.statement: The text says the beans matter but the water temperature does not.
items.explanation: False — the last paragraph lists the beans, the grind, the temperature and the time together.

items.prompt: If you leave the coffee too long, it tastes ___.
items.explanation: Bitter is the sharp, unpleasant taste of over-brewed or burnt coffee. Mild is the opposite of strong.

items.prompt: Throw away the wet ___ when you finish.
items.explanation: The grounds are the wet coffee left after brewing. Beans are what you grind before.

items.prompt: A good ___ of thumb is two tablespoons per cup.
items.explanation: A rule of thumb is a simple approximate rule.

items.prompt: Please ___ the beans just before you make the coffee.
items.explanation: You grind beans into powder; you brew the coffee afterwards.

items.prompt: I don't like strong coffee — I prefer it ___.

discussion: How do you make coffee or tea at home? Explain your method in five steps, using 'first', 'next', 'then' and 'finally'.
Coffee is a daily habit for many Americans. What is the equivalent daily habit where you live?
Explain how to cook or make something you know well, in about eight sentences. Use imperatives: 'Add…', 'Heat…', 'Wait…'.
Do small details really change the result, in cooking or in your own work? Give an example.
